title: Garuda Indonesia 708
summary: A Lockheed L-188C Electra crashed on landing at Mapanget Airport in Manado after a multi-segment domestic flight. Bad weather at Makassar forced a return to Surabaya, and the flight continued the next day. On approach to runway 18 with cloud base at 900 feet and 2 km visibility, the captain realized the aircraft was too high and left of centerline after passing over a hill. The nose was lowered and aircraft banked right, but airspeed decreased below 125 knots, the aircraft landed 156 feet short of the runway threshold with right bank, causing the undercarriage to collapse.
probable_cause: Awkward landing technique resulting in excessive rate of sink on touchdown. Contributing factors were uneven pavement of the runway and marginal weather conditions at landing.

title: South African Airways 406
summary: A Vickers Viscount operating South African Airways Flight 406 crashed into the sea on approach to East London on 13 March 1967, killing all 25 occupants. The cause was never determined. The official investigation speculated without evidence that Captain Lipawsky suffered a heart attack on approach while the first officer was unable to regain control. A later investigator, Judge Cecil Margo, theorized the crash resulted from in-flight structural failure of a wing spar, connecting it to similar Viscount crashes over water with unknown causes.
probable_cause: The cause was not determined. The official investigation speculated the captain suffered a heart attack while on approach and the first officer could not regain control, though a later investigator proposed structural failure from a failed wing spar.

factors.evidence: The investigation considered spatial disorientation possible but believed it unlikely due to the pilot's experience level.

Judge Margo later stated he believed the plane crashed due to separation of the wing from a failed wing spar.
The plane crashing into the sea at night complicated the investigation

title: 1967 Nicosia Britannia disaster
summary: The Bristol Britannia was operating a charter flight bringing tourists from Bangkok in Thailand to Basel in Switzerland. After stopovers in Colombo and Bombay, the crew diverted the flight to Nicosia due to bad weather at Cairo. On the third attempt to land on Runway 32 in a violent thunderstorm, the aircraft flew into a hill near the village of Lakatamia and burst into flames. At the time of the crash, both pilots had exceeded their authorized duty time by three hours. The flight's first officer had less than 50 hours flying time in Britannia aircraft.
probable_cause: Pilot fatigue and limited crew experience on aircraft type in violent thunderstorm conditions during landing approach. Both pilots had exceeded their authorized duty time by three hours and the first officer had minimal experience on the Britannia.

title: 1967 Air Ferry DC-4 accident
summary: A Douglas DC-4 charter flight carrying 83 passengers and 5 crew on a 15-day package holiday was descending to land at Perpignan when it crashed into Mount Canigó at 9,000 feet. The aircraft had reported all was well with good visibility moments before impact. The French Ministry of Transport investigation determined the crash resulted from a series of crew errors caused by carbon monoxide poisoning from a faulty cabin heater.
probable_cause: Controlled flight into terrain caused by pilot incapacitation from carbon monoxide poisoning due to faulty cabin heater. Contributing factors included irrational crew behavior from CO poisoning and language difficulties between crew and French air traffic control.

title: Stockport air disaster
summary: British Midland Flight 542, a Canadair C-4 Argonaut returning holidaymakers from Palma de Mallorca to Manchester, lost its No. 3 and 4 engines over Stockport during a second approach after an earlier overshoot; the No. 4 propeller feathered but the No. 3 kept windmilling, and the aircraft became uncontrollable and crashed at Hopes Carr, killing 72 of 84 aboard. Ruptured fuel tanks fed a fire through the cabin. The AIB found the double engine failure was caused by fuel starvation from an unrecognised flaw in the Argonaut's cross-feed fuel system, with poorly placed cockpit selectors; crew fatigue after a nearly 13-hour duty day was a third contributory factor.
probable_cause: The AIB found the double engine failure resulted from fuel starvation caused by an unrecognised flaw in the Argonaut's fuel cross-feed system, whose poorly placed, unclear cockpit selectors could cause inadvertent cross-feed and exhaust a pair of tanks; crew fatigue was a contributory factor.

title: Piedmont Airlines 22
summary: A Piedmont Airlines Boeing 727 collided with a Cessna 310 at 6,100 feet over Hendersonville, North Carolina. Both aircraft were operating under IFR on different frequencies in radio contact with the Asheville control tower. The 727 was still climbing when the collision occurred just aft of the 727's cockpit. Both aircraft were destroyed and all 82 aboard killed, including John T. McNaughton.
probable_cause: The Cessna pilot's actions were the primary cause, with air traffic control procedures cited as a contributing factor.

title: Cyprus Airways 284
summary: Flight 284 departed Athens at 04:30 bound for Nicosia. About 45 minutes into the flight at 29,000 feet approximately 100 miles southeast of Rhodes, the aircraft exploded. Investigation determined the aircraft had suffered damage during an initial radio call to Nicosia ATC and had disintegrated in flight. A seat cushion fragment contained evidence of military-grade plastic explosive, confirming a bomb destroyed the aircraft.
probable_cause: Bomb explosion in the aircraft cabin at cruise altitude.

title: Aeroflot 2230
summary: Aeroflot Flight 2230, an Ilyushin Il-18V flying from Sverdlovsk to Tashkent, suffered an engine fire shortly after takeoff on 16 November 1967, and the propeller could not be feathered. Maneuverability at maximum takeoff weight was degraded by the drag of the windmilling propeller, and the crew lost control at a height of 200 m while climbing. The aircraft crashed into a plowed field in a 37-degree right bank at 440 km/h, killing all 107 aboard; the wreckage's complete disintegration complicated the investigation.

title: TWA 128
summary: Flight 128 crashed on final approach to Greater Cincinnati Airport at night with the glide slope inoperative. The crew descended to 875 feet before striking trees, attempting a visual approach without adequate altimeter cross-checking. Seventy of the eighty-two people aboard were killed. The NTSB determined the likely cause to be crew error in attempting the visual approach without maintaining minimum altitude.
probable_cause: Crew error, in attempting a visual no-glide-slope approach at night during deteriorating weather conditions, without an adequate altimeter cross-reference.
